title: Kolmogorov complexity
text: Shannon entropy measures the information in a random source: how many binary digits, on average, its outcomes need. Kolmogorov complexity measures the information in one string: the length of the shortest program that prints it. This page defines Kolmogorov complexity, shows that most strings cannot be compressed and that no program computes it, and shows that its expected value per symbol approaches the entropy. It builds on the entropy and source coding pages in Information Theory for Data Science.

title: Kolmogorov complexity
text:
1 Shortest descriptions








Definition 1 (Kolmogorov complexity) Fix a universal computer \(U\): a Turing machine, or an interpreter for a programming language, that reads a program \(p\), a finite string of binary digits, and either runs forever or halts and outputs a binary string \(U(p)\). Assume no program on which \(U\) halts is a proper prefix of another, as happens when \(U\) reads its program one digit at a time and must itself decide where the program ends.
The Kolmogorov complexity of a binary string \(x\) is the length of a shortest program that outputs \(x\):
\[K(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\min \{ \mathopen{}\left|p\right|\mathclose{} : U(p) = x \},\]
where \(\mathopen{}\left|p\right|\mathclose{}\) is the number of digits in \(p\). The conditional Kolmogorov complexity \(K(x \mid n)\) is defined the same way, except that \(U\) is also given the integer \(n\) as an input. This is the definition of Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 14.2).











Theorem 1 (The choice of computer changes \(K\) by at most a constant) Let \(K_U\) and \(K_A\) be the Kolmogorov complexities defined with universal computers \(U\) and \(A\). There is a constant \(c_A\), which depends on \(U\) and \(A\) but not on \(x\), such that
\[K_U(x) \le K_A(x) + c_A \quad \text{for every binary string } x.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Because \(U\) is universal, some program \(s_A\) makes \(U\) simulate \(A\): given \(s_A\) followed by a program \(p\) for \(A\), \(U\) outputs whatever \(A\) outputs on \(p\). So if \(p\) is a shortest program for \(x\) on \(A\), then \(s_A\) followed by \(p\) is a program for \(x\) on \(U\), and \(K_U(x) \le \mathopen{}\left|s_A\right|\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left|p\right|\mathclose{} = K_A(x) + \mathopen{}\left|s_A\right|\mathclose{}\). Take \(c_A = \mathopen{}\left|s_A\right|\mathclose{}\). Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 14.2) give this argument in full.











Remark 1 (Why the choice of computer hardly matters). Applying Theorem 1 with the roles of \(U\) and \(A\) swapped gives a constant \(c'_A\) with \(K_A(x) \le K_U(x) + c'_A\). Together, \(\mathopen{}\left|K_U(x) - K_A(x)\right|\mathclose{} \le \max(c_A, c'_A)\) for every \(x\). The constant can be large, so the complexity of one short string means little, but statements about how \(K(x)\) grows with the length of \(x\) do not depend on the computer. From here on, \(U\) is fixed and dropped from the notation.











Theorem 2 (A string is never much more complex than its length) There is a constant \(c\) such that every binary string \(x\) of length \(n\) has
\[K(x \mid n) \le n + c\]
and, when \(n \ge 1\),
\[K(x) \le n + 2 \log_2 n + c.\]










ProofProof






Proof. For the first bound, the program “print the next \(n\) digits” followed by the \(n\) digits of \(x\) outputs \(x\). Because \(U\) is given \(n\), the program needs no marker to show where it ends, and its fixed part has some length \(c_1\). So \(K(x \mid n) \le n + c_1\).
For the second bound, the program must also describe \(n\) in a way that shows where the description ends. Write \(n\) in binary, which takes \(\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1\) digits, repeat each digit twice, and end with the pair \(01\). This takes \(2 \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 4 \le 2 \log_2 n + 4\) digits. A program that reads this description of \(n\) and then prints the next \(n\) digits has length at most \(n + 2 \log_2 n + 4 + c_2\) for a constant \(c_2\). Take \(c = \max(c_1, c_2 + 4)\). Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 14.2) prove both bounds.











Example 1 (Simple strings)  

The string of \(n\) zeros has \(K(x \mid n) \le c\) for a constant \(c\), since the program “print \(n\) zeros” does not grow with \(n\). Without \(n\) given, the program must also describe \(n\), and the proof of Theorem 2 gives \(K(x) \le 2 \log_2 n + c'\).
The string \(0101\ldots01\) of length \(n\), for even \(n\), also has \(K(x \mid n) \le c\), since the program “print \(01\) until \(n\) digits are printed” does not grow with \(n\). Half its digits are ones, as expected of \(n\) fair coin flips.
The first \(n\) binary digits of \(\pi\) also have \(K(x \mid n) \le c\): a fixed program computes as many digits of \(\pi\) as asked. The digits show no obvious pattern, yet they are as compressible as a string of zeros.

title: Kolmogorov complexity
text:
2 Incompressible strings








Theorem 3 (Most strings are incompressible) Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(0 \le k \le n\) be integers. Fewer than \(2^{n-k}\) of the \(2^n\) binary strings of length \(n\) satisfy \(K(x \mid n) < n - k\). In particular, at least one string of length \(n\) has \(K(x \mid n) \ge n\).










ProofProof






Proof. There are \(2^j\) binary strings of length \(j\), so the number of programs of length less than \(n - k\) is
\[\sum_{j=0}^{n-k-1} 2^j = 2^{n-k} - 1.\]
Given \(n\), each program outputs at most one string, so at most \(2^{n-k} - 1\) strings \(x\) have a program shorter than \(n - k\). With \(k = 0\), at most \(2^n - 1\) of the \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\) have \(K(x \mid n) < n\), which leaves at least one with \(K(x \mid n) \ge n\).











Remark 2 (Incompressible strings look random). By Theorem 3, if \(x\) is drawn uniformly from the strings of length \(n\), for example by \(n\) fair coin flips, then \(\operatorname{P}(K(x \mid n) < n - k) < 2^{n-k} / 2^n = 2^{-k}\). So a string of \(n\) fair coin flips can be compressed by more than \(k\) digits with probability less than \(2^{-k}\). A string with \(K(x \mid n) \ge n\) has no description shorter than itself. Li and Vitányi (2019, chap. 2) call a string random when it is incompressible in this sense, for a variant of \(K\) whose programs need not be prefix-free. A proof can pick an incompressible string and show that some property must hold for it, or else the string would have a short description. Li and Vitányi (2019, chap. 6) call this the incompressibility method.

title: Kolmogorov complexity
text:
3 Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable








Theorem 4 (Kolmogorov complexity cannot be computed) No program takes a binary string \(x\) as input and outputs \(K(x)\).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose a program \(Q\) outputs \(K(x)\) on input \(x\). For each integer \(m \ge 1\), consider the program \(P_m\) that does the following: list binary strings in order of length, use \(Q\) to compute \(K(x)\) for each one, and output the first \(x\) with \(K(x) \ge m\). Such an \(x\) exists, because fewer than \(2^m\) programs are shorter than \(m\), so \(P_m\) halts, and its output \(x\) has \(K(x) \ge m\).
The program \(P_m\) consists of a fixed part, of some length \(c\), and a description of \(m\) that shows where it ends, which the proof of Theorem 2 writes in at most \(2 \log_2 m + 4\) digits. So the output \(x\) of \(P_m\) also has \(K(x) \le 2 \log_2 m + 4 + c\), and together
\[m \le K(x) \le 2 \log_2 m + 4 + c.\]
The left side grows faster than the right, so this fails once \(m\) is large enough, and no such \(Q\) exists. The argument formalizes the Berry paradox, “the smallest positive integer not definable in under sixty letters”, and Cover and Thomas (2006, chap. 14) discuss why \(K\) cannot be computed.

title: Kolmogorov complexity
text:
4 Kolmogorov complexity and entropy








Theorem 5 (Expected Kolmogorov complexity per symbol approaches the entropy) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be independent copies of a random variable \(X\) that takes values in a finite set \(\mathcal{X}\), each value written as a fixed-length binary string, and let \(H_2(X)\) be the entropy of \(X\) with base-2 logarithms. Write \(X^n = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)\). There is a constant \(c\) such that, for every \(n \ge 1\),
\[
H_2(X)
\le \frac{1}{n} \operatorname{E}\left[K(X^n \mid n)\right]
\le H_2(X) + \frac{(\mathopen{}\left|\mathcal{X}\right|\mathclose{} - 1) \log_2 n}{n} + \frac{c}{n}.
\]
So \(\frac{1}{n} \operatorname{E}[K(X^n \mid n)] \to H_2(X)\) as \(n \to \infty\). This is Theorem 14.3.1 of Cover and Thomas (2006).










ProofProof






Proof. For the lower bound, send each outcome \(x^n\) of \(X^n\) to a shortest program that outputs it given \(n\). Different outcomes get different programs, because a program determines its output, and no halting program is a prefix of another, so this is a prefix code for \(X^n\), which makes it uniquely decodable. Its expected length is \(\operatorname{E}[K(X^n \mid n)]\). If \(X\) takes only one value with positive probability, then \(H_2(X) = 0\) and the lower bound holds trivially. Otherwise, \(X^n\) also takes at least two values with positive probability, and part 1 of the source coding theorem gives \(\operatorname{E}[K(X^n \mid n)] \ge H_2(X^n)\). Applying the chain rule for entropy \(n - 1\) times, and using that conditioning on independent variables does not change entropy, gives \(H_2(X^n) = n H_2(X)\). Dividing by \(n\) gives the lower bound.
For the upper bound, Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 14.3) describe \(x^n\) in two parts: first how many times each value in \(\mathcal{X}\) occurs, which takes about \((\mathopen{}\left|\mathcal{X}\right|\mathclose{} - 1) \log_2 n\) digits, then which of the strings with those counts \(x^n\) is, which takes about \(n H_2(X)\) digits on average.











Remark 3 (Entropy describes a distribution; Kolmogorov complexity describes a string). Entropy is the expected surprisal of a random variable, so it is a property of a distribution and says nothing about any one outcome. Kolmogorov complexity is a property of one string and needs no distribution. Theorem 5 says that the two agree on average, per symbol, for long independent sequences. For a single string they can disagree: the string \(0101\ldots01\) in Example 1 has as many ones as zeros, like a typical outcome of fair coin flips, whose entropy is 1 bit per flip, but its Kolmogorov complexity per digit, \(K(x \mid n)/n \le c/n\), tends to 0.

text:

title: Asymptotic notation
text: The cost of an algorithm depends on the size \(n\) of its input. Asymptotic notation compares how two costs grow as \(n\) grows, ignoring constant factors and small inputs.

title: Asymptotic notation
text:
1 Upper, lower and tight bounds








Definition 1 (Big-O notation) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the positive integers to \([0, \infty)\). We write \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if there are a constant \(c > 0\) and an integer \(n_0\) such that
\[f(n) \le c \, g(n) \quad \text{for every } n \ge n_0.\]
That is, \(f\) grows no faster than a constant multiple of \(g\) once \(n\) is large enough. This is the definition of Arora and Barak (2009, sec. 0.3).











Definition 2 (Big-Omega notation) For \(f\) and \(g\) as in Definition 1, we write \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) if there are a constant \(c > 0\) and an integer \(n_0\) such that
\[f(n) \ge c \, g(n) \quad \text{for every } n \ge n_0.\]
Dividing by \(c\) shows that this holds exactly when \(g(n) = O(f(n))\), with constant \(1/c\).











Definition 3 (Big-Theta notation) For \(f\) and \(g\) as in Definition 1, we write \(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\) if both \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) (Definition 1) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) (Definition 2). Then \(f\) and \(g\) grow at the same rate, up to constant factors.











Remark 1 (The equals sign is one-way). \(O(g(n))\) stands for a set of functions, and \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) says that \(f\) belongs to it. So \(n = O(n^2)\) is true, but \(n^2 = O(n)\) is false, and the statement cannot be read from right to left. Cormen et al. (2009, sec. 3.1) reads the notation this way.

title: Asymptotic notation
text:
2 Examples








Example 1 (A quadratic is \(O(n^2)\) but not \(O(n)\)) Let \(f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n\).
For \(n \ge 5\), we have \(5n \le n \cdot n = n^2\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(n)
&= 3n^2 + 5n \\
&\le 3n^2 + n^2 \\
&= 4n^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(f(n) = O(n^2)\), with \(c = 4\) and \(n_0 = 5\) in Definition 1. Since \(f(n) \ge 3n^2\) for every \(n\), also \(f(n) = \Omega(n^2)\) (Definition 2), and so \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) (Definition 3).
But \(f(n)\) is not \(O(n)\). If it were, there would be \(c > 0\) and \(n_0\) with \(3n^2 + 5n \le c \, n\) for every \(n \ge n_0\). Dividing both sides by \(n > 0\) gives \(3n + 5 \le c\) for every \(n \ge n_0\), which fails for any \(n\) larger than both \(n_0\) and \((c - 5)/3\).











Example 2 (Counting the operations in an inner product) The inner product of two vectors \(\tilde{x}, \tilde{z}\in \mathbb{R}^D\) is
\[\tilde{x}^\top \tilde{z}= x_1 z_1 + x_2 z_2 + \cdots + x_D z_D.\]
Computing it takes \(D\) multiplications, one for each product \(x_d z_d\), and \(D - 1\) additions to sum the \(D\) products: \(2D - 1\) arithmetic operations in all. Since \(2D - 1 \le 2D\) for every \(D \ge 1\), the cost is \(O(D)\), with \(D\) in the role of \(n\), \(c = 2\) and \(n_0 = 1\) in Definition 1. Since \(2D - 1 \ge D\) for every \(D \ge 1\), it is also \(\Omega(D)\) (Definition 2), so it is \(\Theta(D)\) (Definition 3). When a machine learning text says an inner product “costs \(O(D)\)”, it means this count of operations, up to a constant factor.

text:
References


Arora, Sanjeev, and Boaz Barak. 2009. Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804090.

title: Computational Complexity for Data Science
text:
Computational complexity asks how much time, memory or randomness a problem needs, whatever algorithm solves it. Data science meets it whenever fitting a model exactly turns out to be computationally hard, which is one reason practical methods use greedy search or a convex surrogate loss.
These notes collect the computational complexity that data science courses use. They are new. The pages written so far are:

Asymptotic notation: big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta, and what it means for a computation to cost \(O(D)\)
Kolmogorov complexity: the length of the shortest program that prints a string, why most strings are incompressible and no program computes it, and how its average per symbol approaches Shannon entropy

The planned topics still to come are:

models of computation: Turing machines and computability
time and space complexity, and the classes P and NP
reductions and NP-completeness
randomized computation
communication and information complexity

Information theory has its own library, Information Theory for Data Science. Results that connect the two live in the library that holds their main statement, and the other links to them.

title: Computational Complexity for Data Science
text:
Starting materials
These notes are written fresh, but they draw on the following books and Stanford course pages.

Sanjeev Arora and Boaz Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, the main starting point for complexity theory.
CS154: Introduction to the Theory of Computation (Omer Reingold and Li-Yang Tan), which covers automata, computability and complexity, using Michael Sipser’s Introduction to the Theory of Computation, with lecture slides and videos.
CS154: Introduction to Automata and Complexity Theory (Spring 2009, with Rajeev Motwani among the course staff), with handouts, homework and a reading list.
Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, Jeff Ullman’s home page for the book, which is the textbook the 2009 CS154 page links. It has solutions to starred exercises, errata, slides, and past CS154 course materials.
CS254: Computational Complexity (Li-Yang Tan), which covers space complexity, the polynomial hierarchy, randomized and non-uniform computation, and interactive proofs. It uses Arora and Barak and Avi Wigderson’s Mathematics and Computation, and links a reading for each lecture.

section: Using these notes in another site
text:
Using these notes in another site
Course sites link to these pages by URL; they do not include this repository as a git submodule. A host site that keeps a copy of this repository at its root, named cds, can still include fragments with paths that start with cds/. This site includes its own fragments the same way, through a cds symlink that points at the repository root.
Quarto resolves @id cross-references only within one rendered page, so a host site that links to a result here uses an explicit link to the page and anchor.
